sections.mechanism_or_content: Defines rooted honeycomb SAW counts c_n, submultiplicative connective constant μ, mid-edge partition function Z(x), critical fugacity x_c=1/μ, and states Theorem 1. The physical rendering of p.2 verifies μ=√(2+√2), which PDF text extraction drops a radical from.

sections.unit: §2 Parafermionic observable, Definition 1, Lemma 1 and proof
sections.mechanism_or_content: On simply connected finite domains, defines F(z)=Σ exp(-iσW)x^ℓ; at x=x_c and σ=5/8 proves the local three-mid-edge relation by pairing paths visiting all three incident mid-edges and grouping one-edge/two-edge extensions into triplets. Figure 1 fixes the winding convention; Figure 2 depicts the two cancellations.

sections.unit: §3 Counting argument in a strip and proof of Theorem 1
sections.mechanism_or_content: Sums the local relation over a finite strip to obtain 1=c_αA_T+B_T+c_εE_T with c_α=cos(3π/8), c_ε=cos(π/4); passes to infinite height. Either some E_T>0 makes Z(x_c)=∞, or E_T=0 for every T and the bridge partition functions satisfy a harmonic lower bound through A_{T+1}-A_T≤x_c B_{T+1}². For x<x_c, canonical decreasing-width bridge decomposition bounds Z(x) by 2∏_T(1+B_T(x))²<∞. Figures 3-4 show the domain and bridge decomposition.

Records the proved critical bridge bounds and then separates exponent/SLE scaling predictions from the theorem. Conjecture 1 is chordal SAW convergence to SLE(8/3); Conjecture 2 is a normalized observable limit. The paper explicitly says the local relation alone does not determine the observable's scaling limit.
Read complete bibliography and end matter; confirms cited sources and article termination.

sections.unit: Abstract, §1 Introduction, definitions, results and structure
sections.mechanism_or_content: Defines rooted SAWs on Z² and H, bridge and polygon counts, line-width, and polygon convention. States Hammersley-Welsh, square-lattice subsequential improvement, honeycomb all-large-n improvement, and the separate conditional universal-cover polynomial bound. Lemma 1.5 is the multi-valued-map counting inequality; Lemma 1.6 converts bridge pairs into polygons.

sections.unit: §2.1-2.2 Hammersley-Welsh bridge lists and unfolding proof
sections.mechanism_or_content: Strictly decreasing bridge heights and integer-partition counting give exp(C√n) multiplicity; record-point decomposition injects half-space walks into bridge lists, and cutting at the final minimum reduces arbitrary walks to half-space walks.

Identifies many tall-branch near-touches in horizontally confined walks and explains polygon insertion as a many-valued perturbation of the Hammersley-Welsh map. Separates insertion-slot entropy from scarcity |WSAP_m^u|μ^-m and derives the heuristic exponent restrictions; this overview is not the rigorous proof. Figures 1-2 illustrate the cover and local surgery.

sections.unit: §3.1 Polygon definitions, abundance on Z², and proof of Proposition 3.1
sections.mechanism_or_content: Defines wide polygons by line-width≥u and height≤16u. Lemma 3.3 bins polygon diameter, uses bridge-to-polygon counting and an injective plaquette join, then Cauchy-Schwarz over matching heights; divergence of the critical bridge generating series yields a subsequence abundance bound for every α>29. Proposition 3.2 states the stronger all-u honeycomb abundance bound for later proof.

sections.unit: §3.2 Madras joining, Lemma 3.4 and application notation
sections.mechanism_or_content: Reviews local polygon-polygon/bridge-polygon surgery. Under vertical containment (3.4), the Z² join remains a bridge, increases length by m+16, has junction-edge chemical distance m+7, preserves all but at most two branch edges, commutes for vertically separated insertions, and has at most four presurgical inputs per output/junction.

sections.unit: §4 Polygon insertion reduction, Proposition 4.1 and proof of Theorem 1.2
sections.mechanism_or_content: Sets the parameter restrictions, reduces to horizontally confined walks with many branches, and proves the square-lattice exponent result from Proposition 4.4 plus subsequential polygon abundance. The long-range statement covers every n in [j,j^(4/3)] for infinitely many j; it does not assert the bound at all n.

sections.unit: §5.1-5.2 Tall branches, viable joins, and multi-valued-map bounds
sections.mechanism_or_content: Defines the rectangle, tall crossings, viable join indices and separated join-location lists. Lemmas 5.1-5.2 prove overlap with the adjacent branch and quantify the number of choices; Lemma 5.3 bounds outgoing arrows below and incoming multiplicity above. Proposition 4.4 follows by the multi-valued-map inequality.

sections.unit: §5.3-5.5 Construction, inverse recovery, and limitations of Φ
sections.mechanism_or_content: Iterates Madras joins at separated heights, then recovers surgeries from self-intersections in the unfolded non-self-avoiding output. Right-detachable adjacency Lemma 5.5 controls ambiguity; at most twelve choices per insertion give multiplicity 12^(κr) on Z². The final subsection discusses parameter/abundance limits and possible refinements. Figures 5-6 illustrate surgery and the planar recovery argument.

sections.unit: §6.1-6.3 Honeycomb model definitions, observable, and Proposition 3.2 proof
sections.mechanism_or_content: Defines rooted oriented midpoint-walks and polygon traces on H, critical two-point function, and the σ=5/8 parafermionic relation. Boundary winding turns the observable identity into positive partition-function identities in a strip and triangle. Three crossing walks are concatenated in an upper half-plane domain and paired with a reflection to create round polygons; the O(u²) possible lengths and at most 16u representatives per trace yield the u^-10 abundance. Figures 8-9 identify the geometry.

sections.unit: §7.1-7.3 Universal-cover setup, roadmap and first reduction
sections.mechanism_or_content: Defines branch-cut, universal and 8-fold covers and the polygonal domains Λ_k. Theorem 1.4 assumes a k with μ(U_k^∞)=μ(H). Proposition 7.1 reduces the count to a polynomial bound for two-point functions; Lemma 7.2 uses the 8-fold cover and an observable boundary relation.

Proves the cover observable estimate, constructs outer paths of length O(n²) with weight at least c n^-103 between lifted boundary points, and decomposes inner walks into excursions to manufacture polygons avoiding Λ_k. The map multiplicity and 6k+7 polygon factors give the corollary. Figures 10-11 display the path and join geometry.

sections.unit: §7.7-7.8 Polynomial polygon bound and general Proposition 7.1
sections.mechanism_or_content: Under equality of the universal-cover connective constant with μ(H), good polygons in U_k^∞ have exponential growth at most μ(H); joining a polygon with useful planar polygons makes it good with controlled polynomial multiplicity. This yields a polynomial two-point bound and completes the conditional theorem for arbitrary interior endpoints. The result is conditional on Conjecture 1 or the weaker good-polygon growth condition.

sections.unit: Appendix A.1-A.3 Hexagonal Madras join and theorem transfer
sections.mechanism_or_content: Defines the H-lattice face-based join; join length increases by m+18 (not m+16), the junction hexagon replaces the square plaquette, and chemical distance is m+3. Appendix A.3 explains the α threshold change 29→10, all-u polygon availability, and inverse multiplicity L(H)=3. Figure 12 appears on physical p.53 and Figure 13 on p.54.
Read complete bibliography and end matter; article references span both physical pages.

sections.unit: Abstract and §1.1-1.6 Model, definitions, theorems and comparison
sections.mechanism_or_content: Defines iid Bernoulli bond dilution on Z^d, rooted n-step SAW count Z_N and annealed p^N s_N, then states Proposition 1.1 and Theorem 1.4. The central quenched quantity is limsup Z_N(x)^(1/N); Remark 1.2 explicitly leaves existence of the full limit as a conjecture. The strict separation theorem is planar, p∈(1/2,1), and compares against the unconditioned environment expectation.

sections.unit: §2.1 Proof of Proposition 1.1: root independence and nonrandomness
sections.mechanism_or_content: For neighboring roots, decomposes walks by first hit of the neighboring vertex and bounds counts by convolutions of rooted counts; limsup nth-root growth is therefore root invariant. Finite environment changes preserve the rate by edge/pendant-vertex operations; the rate is tail measurable and Kolmogorov's zero-one law makes it deterministic.

Couples p<p' percolations by common iid uniforms. Conditional expectation given the denser environment gives E[Z_N(ω_p)|F_p']=(p/p')^N Z_N(ω_p'); Markov plus Borel-Cantelli yields μ_d(p)/μ_d(p')≤p/p'.

Explains fractional moments/coarse graining; Proposition 3.1 assumes dν_d<2 and only proves Z_N/E Z_N→0 in probability, not exponentially. A spatially inhomogeneous Bernoulli tilt in a box of radius N^α makes the confined contribution small while its Radon–Nikodym cost remains bounded.

sections.unit: §3.3 Animal decomposition and fractional moment reduction
sections.mechanism_or_content: Partitions edges into N_0-boxes, maps each SAW to its connected lattice animal, uses (Σa_i)^θ≤Σa_i^θ and a_m≤49^m, then reduces the theorem to a per-animal θ=1/2 estimate. Equations (3.23)-(3.26) show the resulting strict connective-constant gap.

Lemma 3.3 is Cauchy-Schwarz for arbitrary positive f_A. For small m, lowers edge-open intensity blockwise; the inverse-density cost grows at most 10^m while the tilted path weight falls as 10^-5m once C_2 is large.

sections.unit: §3.6 Large-animal case and completion of Theorem 1.4
sections.mechanism_or_content: Select separated blocks and use a weighted centered quadratic form Q_x with 1/d(e,e') kernel. Its variance is uniformly bounded, while conditioning on a path being open forces its mean to grow like (1-p)log N_0; Chebyshev bounds the tilted expectation. Combined with the fractional moment and Borel-Cantelli this gives μ_2(p)≤4^(-1/N_0²)pμ_2(1)<pμ_2(1), with N_0=exp(C_2/(1-p)²).
Repeats the animal/change-of-measure argument starting from a p'-dilute graph and parameter q=p/p', proving strict monotonicity rather than only nondecrease of the ratio in dimension two.

sections.unit: §5.1-5.4 Self-avoiding walk in an iid random potential
sections.mechanism_or_content: For iid mean-zero unit-variance site potentials with finite log-mgf for every real parameter, proves limsup quenched free-energy growth is strictly below annealed growth for β≠0. Uses FKG to reduce to small β, animal coarse graining, linear tilt for small animals, and a quadratic-form tilt for large animals. This is a separate site-potential model, not the percolation theorem.

sections.unit: §6 Site percolation and lattice trees/animals extensions
sections.mechanism_or_content: States adaptations to site percolation and to lattice trees, including an analogous limsup strict separation; these are extension claims with model-specific definitions and are not needed for edge-SAW C108.
Read complete 31-item bibliography and end matter.

sections.unit: Front matter, abstract, contents, and foreword
sections.mechanism_or_content: Verified arXiv v1/title/authors and full contents map. Abstract identifies the chapter scope: Hammersley–Welsh bridges/polygons, exact honeycomb connective constant, high-dimensional lace expansion, and integral representation/4D RG.

Defines strict/weak SAW, rooted counts and connective constant; states elementary submultiplicativity, numerical/conjectural exponents, exact theorem dependencies and model caveats. Separates proven d≥5 strict-SAW results from predictions in d=2,3,4 and from continuous-time weak-SAW RG. Includes exercises on random-walk comparison and intersection integrals.

For nearest-neighbor Z^d strict SAW, defines bridges, half-space walks and spans; strictly decreasing bridge heights encode partitions. Theorem 2.4 on physical p.12 gives log P_D(A)~pi*sqrt(A/3). Theorem 2.6 on p.13 uses two partition factors in the last-minimum split of an arbitrary SAW, producing the larger B>pi*sqrt(2/3) threshold. Bridge growth equals mu; polygon concatenation and the bridge-pair injection/Cauchy–Schwarz yield polygon growth mu.

With midpoint walks on the honeycomb lattice, proves μ_H=√(2+√2). A winding-weighted observable at σ=5/8 and x_c=1/μ_H has a local three-mid-edge relation by pair/triplet path cancellation; summed strip-boundary identities give divergence at x_c and finite susceptibility below it. Sections 3.3–3.4 explicitly present SAW-to-SLE and O(n) phase claims as conjectural/predicted, separate from the exact connective-constant theorem.

sections.unit: §4 Lace expansion: differential inequality and inclusion–exclusion derivation
sections.mechanism_or_content: States previously proved nearest-neighbor strict-SAW mean-field theorems for d≥5 (not proved in full in this chapter). Derives the fixed-length lace recursion by repeated inclusion–exclusion and compatible-lace decomposition, Fourier-transforming to the two-point denominator. The bubble condition on Σ_x G_z(x)^2 implies linear susceptibility divergence via d(zχ)/dz≥χ²/Bubble. Completes the formal/tutorial development through the start of §5.

Bounds lace terms by diagrammatic norms; uses a simple-random-walk comparison and bootstrap/continuity to prove critical bubble finiteness when β is small. Nearest-neighbor β≤K/(d−4) gives sufficiently high dimensions; spread-out β≤K L^(−d) works for d>4 at sufficiently large L. Corollary 5.4 yields χ(z) asymp (1−z/zc)^(−1). Proof details are partly sketched/referred to the lace-expansion literature.

sections.unit: §6 Integral representations: Gaussian and differential-form identities
sections.mechanism_or_content: Builds the finite-volume boson/fermion representation. Gaussian integrations generate a SAW with loop background; Grassmann/differential forms self-normalize the residual product and eliminate loops. Theorem 6.11 Eq. (6.43), physical p.48, is the identity sum_{omega in S_ab(Lambda)} C_omega = integral e^{-S_A} bar(phi_a)phi_b product_{x in Lambda\{a,b}}(1+tau_x), for finite Lambda and C=A^{-1} with positive Hermitian part. Definition 6.4 specifies the form integral; this is not a scalar pointwise identity or an infinite-volume asymptotic theorem.

Defines rate-2d continuous-time SRW, local times L_v,T, weight exp(−g Σ_v L_v,T²), critical ν_c(g), and states the critical two-point asymptotic for d≥4 and sufficiently small g≥0. The theorem is attributed to Brydges–Slade; section compares hierarchical-lattice and long-range results without transferring them to strict planar SAW.

Theorem 7.2 takes a subcritical parameter limit and growing-torus limit to recover the infinite-volume two-point function. Theorem 7.3 gives the finite-volume supersymmetric integral representation, then introduces mass/external-field parameters for the critical asymptotic problem.

Defines Gaussian superexpectation and its convolution property; Theorem 7.5 decomposes the massive torus covariance into finite-range positive-definite covariances with derivative bounds for fixed order p, d>2, sufficiently large dyadic scale L.

sections.unit: §7.6–7.8 Polymer recursion, RG flow, and discrete-time tutorial
sections.mechanism_or_content: Sets up polymer activities and circle products, gives the RG recursion and flow equations as a summary with technical details omitted, and begins the discrete-time weak-SAW Simon–Lieb tutorial. The detailed fixed-point derivation is deferred to cited work; the version bibliography lists one account as in preparation.
Reads solutions to the elementary count/radius/connective-constant, random-walk Fourier Green function and intersection-integrability exercises.

sections.unit: Appendix A.2 Solutions to Tutorial 4.4 (lace expansion)
sections.mechanism_or_content: Works through connected graph/lace decomposition, compatibility sets, and the walk-avoidance patterns for the first several lace orders; identifies which lace intervals may have zero length.

sections.unit: Appendix A.3 Solutions to Tutorial 5.4 (high-dimensional estimates)
sections.mechanism_or_content: Derives Fourier-integral monotonicity, high-dimensional bounds for long SAW segments and first lace coefficients, then the stated 1/d expansion μ=2d−1−(2d)^(−1)+O((2d)^(−2)). These are theorem/exercise calculations under the lace estimates, not finite numerical evidence.

sections.unit: Appendix A.4 Solutions to Tutorial 7.8 (finite-volume approximation)
sections.mechanism_or_content: Proves submultiplicativity for weak-SAW weights, torus comparison, Simon–Lieb inequality, exponential decay, and convergence of finite-torus two-point functions under ν>ν_c.
Read all acknowledgements and bibliography entries through reference [72], plus author affiliations/end matter; no pages omitted.

sections.mechanism_or_content: Defines rooted uniform nearest-neighbor strict SAW on Z^d, d≥2, and prints the prefactor-free exponential tail for maximum Euclidean displacement ≥vn for every n at fixed v>0. The literal n=1,v=1/2 boundary case is impossible; the card preserves the source wording but limits tool use to sufficiently large n or a finite-prefactor form.

Separates predicted mean-square exponents/SLE from proved claims; defines the boundary-to-boundary finite-domain weighted SAW and states critical length corollary. Subcritical fluctuation/geodesic discussion is qualified; supercritical space-filling is cited as a separate result.
States graph-dependent scope/open questions and acknowledges support. Does not prove ballisticity on non-amenable graphs or resolve exponent/tightness questions.

sections.unit: §2 Preliminaries: bridges, irreducibility, theorem roadmap, proof of Theorem 1.1
sections.mechanism_or_content: Defines vertical bridges and renewal points, proves the Hammersley–Welsh walk/bridge comparison and Kesten irreducible-bridge probability identity, and states the ballistic assumption and contradiction roadmap. Under that assumption, Theorem 2.3 gives renewal-rich bridges at subexponential cost along a subsequence; Corollary 2.4 says ballisticity forces finite irreducible-bridge mean, while Theorem 2.5 states the incompatible infinite-mean result. The proof direction for Corollary 2.4 is on physical p.18 in §3 and is recorded there.

sections.unit: §3 Positive density of renewal points at subexponential cost
sections.mechanism_or_content: Theorem 3.1 obtains renewal-rich bridges along a subsubsequence. Proposition 3.2 reduces height-band visits via zigzag unfoldings, with three cases and a multivalued-map/preimage bound; the reduction is explicitly subsequential. The physical p.18 proof of Corollary 2.4 assumes infinite iSAB mean, truncates block lengths, and uses exponential Markov plus the exp(C sqrt(n)) bridge-conditioning loss to bound renewal-rich bridges by exp(-epsilon n+C sqrt(n)); this contradicts Theorem 2.3's subexponential lower cost under ballisticity, so ballisticity forces finite mean.

sections.unit: §4 Incompatibility of bridge renewal theory and stickbreak proof
sections.mechanism_or_content: Constructs stationary ergodic bi-infinite concatenated iSAB paths; finite mean implies positive density of diamond points. Stickbreaks at separated diamond points preserve self-avoidance, add two edges, create a macroscopic width excursion and reduce renewal count. Weighted input/output counting contradicts the finite-mean typical-width law, proving E_iSAB|γ|=∞.

Corollary 1.2 is immediate from Theorem 1.1. Corollary 1.3’s proof is a sketch reducing the critical finite-domain length estimate to subcritical Ornstein–Zernike estimates and divergence of the susceptibility.
